title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Lewis (1975) on language
What are languages?

Lewis: collections of pairs of forms and meanings

Form: sign, sound, mark, etc.
Meaning: set (i.e., collection) of possible states of affairs, things in the world, etc.



What is language?

A human social activity in which people produce certain forms.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Relating them
Lewis introduces a convention to define language use:

“…a population P uses a language ξ is a convention of truthfulness and trust in ξ.”

Truthfulness: try never to utter sentences of ξ that are not true in ξ.
Trust in ξ: impute truthfulness in ξ to others. Believe the things that others tell you.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
“Language use”
These are pragmatic conventions.

What about conventions relating to form?

syntax, morphology, phonology, phonetics, etc.
sociolinguistic conventions: using a particular register/dialect in particular social setting

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Communication and meaning
Grice (1957): conceptual analysis of the word ‘mean’.

This rainy weather means we’ll probably be taxiing for a while.
Jo’s gesture means that she wants you to walk over.
“Bo devoured the beans” means that Bo ate the beans aggressively.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Test 1

This rainy weather means we’ll probably be taxiing for a while, but in fact, we won’t be taxiing for a while.
Jo’s gesture means that she wants you to walk over, but in fact, she doesn’t want you to walk over.
“Bo devoured the beans” means that Bo ate the beans aggressively, but in fact, Bo didn’t eat the beans aggressively.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Test 2

What is meant by this rainy weather is that we’ll be taxiing for a while.
What is meant by Jo’s gesture is that she wants you to walk over.
What is meant by “Bo devoured the beans” is that Bo ate the beans aggressively.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Test 3

Someone meant by this rainy weather that we’ll probably be taxiing for a while.
Jo meant by her gesture that she wants you to walk over.
Someone meant by “Bo devoured the beans” that Bo ate the beans aggressively.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Natural and non-natural meaning

‘mean’ in the 1 examples: describes a consequence relation
‘mean’ in the 2 and 3 examples: some other kind of relation


Grice (1957): natural meaning vs. non-natural meaning.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Non-natural meaning
Hypothesis 1
Something means\(_{NN}\) that \(p\) if things of its kind tend to produce a belief in an observer that \(p\) is true.

sun being out makes people believe it’s daytime…

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Non-natural meaning
Hypothesis 2
Maybe we should factor in intention.

Someone means\(_{NN}\) that \(p\) by something if they intend to use that thing to produce the belief in an audience that \(p\) is true.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text: Counterexample

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Non-natural meaning
Hypothesis 3
Maybe we should factor in an intention for one’s intention to be recognized.

Someone means\(_{NN}\) that \(p\) by something if they intend to produce the belief that \(p\) in their audience by that thing, and they intend for their intention to be recognized.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Counterexample
Cutting someone off in traffic to make them think you’re aggressive and to get them to get out of your way.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Non-natural meaning
What it actually is (according to Grice)

Someone means\(_{NN}\) that \(p\) by something if they intend that:

their audience comes to believe \(p\) because of it,
their audience recognizes their intention, and
their audience comes to believe that \(p\) specifically because of the intention.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:

title: Intro. to Semantics
section: Some things you can do with words
text:
Some things you can do with words

Make assertions:

John devoured the beans.



Ask questions:

How many beans did John devour?



Issue commands:

(Looking John dead in the eye:) Devour the beans!

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Distinguishing types of act
Austin (1962) classified speech acts at distinct levels.

Locutionary act: an act of uttering a particular expression.

e.g., interrogative vs. imperative vs. declarative

Illocutionary act: an an act of uttering something with a particular intended discourse effect.

e.g., question vs. comamand vs. assertion

Perlocutionary effects: the worldly effects an utterance actually has.

e.g., question answered, command fulfilled, assertion believed

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Illocutionary uptake
An illocutionary act may be successful or unsuccessful.

Successful if it has the intended social consequence (it has uptake).
Unsuccessful if it does not have this consequence (it does not have uptake).

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Uptakes for different acts

I bet you $300 that it will rain tomorrow.

the bet is accepted

Open the window!

addressee accepts the obligation to act

What time is it?

addressee accepts the obligation to answer

It’s 1:20pm.

addressee accepts (in some sense) the truth of the sentence

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Assertions
Stalnaker (1978) introduces the notion of the common ground.

set of propositions


Uptake of an assertion:

addressee accepts the meaning of the sentence into the common ground.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Force and content
Illocutionary acts can be characterized along at least two dimensions:

illocutionary force: what kind of intended social effect is involved?

assertoric force, imperative force, interrogative force

content: utterance-specific aspects of conveyed meaning

assertions: sets of possible worlds (“truth conditions”)
commands: “satisfaction conditions”
questions: “answerhood conditions”

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Question about content
Where in the taxonomy of acts does content fall?

Just the illocutionary act?
Also locutionary effect?
(Also perlocutionary effect?)

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Performatives

I command you to help me cook the beans!
I hereby name this ship the R.M.S. Titanic!

locutionary act: declarative sentence
illocutionary act: naming
uptake: ship’s name is now ‘R.M.S. Titanic’

I promise to stop moving furniture while you’re sleeping.

locutionary act: declarative sentence
illocutionary act: promise
uptake: promise accepted, obligation registered

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Peformatives (cont’d)

I apologize.

apology
uptake: apology accepted

I do.

illocutionary act: vow
uptake: obligation registered

I bet you $300 that it will rain tomorrow.

illocutionary act: bet
uptake: bet accepted

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Felicity conditions
You can’t just perform any speech act haphazardly.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Felicity conditions

I apologize.

The speaker should have done something that requires an apology.

I do.

There should be a vow at stake (“…till death do us part?”).

Open the window!

The utterer should have the relevant authority.

I bet you $300 that it will rain tomorrow.

The utterer should have the means to procure $300.

title: Intro. to Semantics
text:
Felicity conditions
In general:

It must be allowable, by convention, for the speech act to have the illocutionary effect that it is intended to have.
The circumstances prior to the act have to be appropriate.
